title: Azure RBAC and Managed Identities
intro: Azure access is 'role assignments': a principal (user, group, service principal, or managed identity) gets a role (Reader, Contributor, Key Vault Secrets User...) at a scope (management group, subscription, resource group, or single resource). Managed identities give Azure resources their own identity, so apps need no secrets.

steps.prompt: Show your own signed-in user's object id.
expected_commands: az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv
steps.explanation: Your Entra ID object id: the value role assignments refer to.
steps.why: Role assignments are keyed by object id, not by name. When an assignment shows up as 'Unknown' in the portal, the principal behind that object id was deleted.

steps.prompt: List every role assignment for alice@contoso.com across all scopes.
expected_commands: az role assignment list --assignee alice@contoso.com --all --output table
az role assignment list --assignee alice@contoso.com --all -o table
steps.fake_output:
Principal          Role         Scope
-----------------  -----------  -------------------------------------------------------------
alice@contoso.com  Reader       /subscriptions/33333333-dddd-4eee-8fff-444444444444
alice@contoso.com  Contributor  /subscriptions/33333333-dddd-4eee-8fff-444444444444/resourceGroups/rg-web-prod
steps.explanation: Reader on the whole prod subscription, Contributor on one resource group.
steps.why: Without --all you only see assignments at the current subscription scope. Also note that permissions inherit downward: Reader on the subscription applies to every group and resource in it. Assign at the smallest scope that does the job.

steps.prompt: Give vm-app-01 (rg-web-prod) a system-assigned managed identity.
expected_commands: az vm identity assign --resource-group rg-web-prod --name vm-app-01
az vm identity assign -g rg-web-prod -n vm-app-01
steps.explanation: The VM now has its own Entra ID identity, with principal id 5e6f7a8b-9c0d-4e1f-8a2b-3c4d5e6f7a8b.
steps.why: Code on the VM gets tokens from the local metadata endpoint, so there's no connection string or client secret to leak or rotate: the same idea as an AWS instance profile. System-assigned identities live and die with the VM; user-assigned ones can be shared and survive the VM.

steps.prompt: Let that identity (5e6f7a8b-9c0d-4e1f-8a2b-3c4d5e6f7a8b) read secrets from the Key Vault kv-web-prod only: assign 'Key Vault Secrets User' scoped to /subscriptions/33333333-dddd-4eee-8fff-444444444444/resourceGroups/rg-web-prod/providers/Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/kv-web-prod.
expected_commands: az role assignment create --assignee 5e6f7a8b-9c0d-4e1f-8a2b-3c4d5e6f7a8b --role "Key Vault Secrets User" --scope /subscriptions/33333333-dddd-4eee-8fff-444444444444/resourceGroups/rg-web-prod/providers/Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/kv-web-prod
steps.explanation: The VM can read secrets from one vault, and do nothing else.
steps.why: Scoping to the single vault rather than the resource group is least privilege in practice. Secrets User can read secret values but not manage the vault. Role assignments can take a few minutes to take effect, so an immediate 403 isn't proof it failed.

steps.prompt: Look up what the built-in role 'Key Vault Secrets User' actually allows.
expected_commands: az role definition list --name "Key Vault Secrets User"
az role definition list --name 'Key Vault Secrets User'
steps.explanation: Only data actions: read secret values and metadata.
steps.why: Azure separates control-plane 'actions' (manage the resource) from data-plane 'dataActions' (use its contents). An Owner of a vault can't read its secrets without a data-plane role. That separation surprises people, and it's exactly the point.
